title: SRE: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, and Runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
content:
## Purpose
This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning practices, ongoing reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical SRE runbooks. It is intended to provide a single, practical reference that service owners and on-call engineers can use to set targets, measure reliability, plan capacity, and respond to incidents in a consistent way.

## Scope
Covers: hosted API endpoints, dedicated inference pools, control plane services (orchestration, routing), and monitoring/alerting pipelines. Does not replace product SLAs or legal contracts; SLAs must be derived from the SLOs in coordination with Legal and Sales.

## Guiding principles
- Keep SLOs consumer-focused: measure behavior that matters to customers (success rate, latency, freshness).
- Make error budgets actionable: use them for release gating, rollbacks, and capacity decisions.
- Automate measurement and reporting: dashboards and alerts must be programmatic.
- Review reliability work regularly: prioritize engineering work to protect remaining error budget and reduce toil.

## SLOs and error budgets
1) Default SLO taxonomy (applies to all public-facing services):
   - Availability/Success-rate SLO: percentage of successful end-to-end requests. Typical target: 99.95% (monthly) for core inference endpoints; lower-tier or non-customer-facing control-plane services 99.9%.
   - Latency SLOs: tail latency for customer experience. Example: p95 < 250 ms for inference-frontend; p99 < 1s for request proxy.
   - Freshness / consistency SLOs: for model rollouts or cache invalidation. Example: 99% of model-traffic switchovers complete within 5 minutes.

2) Error budget calculation (example):
   - SLO = 99.95% monthly.
   - Allowed error rate = 1 - 0.9995 = 0.0005 (0.05%).
   - If monthly requests = 2,000,000, allowed failed requests = 2,000,000 * 0.0005 = 1,000.
   - Track remaining budget daily and project burn rate.

3) Error budget policy (standard):
   - If burn rate > 2x and remaining budget < 50%: immediate mitigation required (throttle releases, reduce non-essential traffic, escalate to SRE manager).
   - If burn rate > 5x or remaining budget < 10%: trigger emergency reliability meeting and rollback any risky deploys.
   - Use error budget to decide on canary promotion windows and capacity increases.

4) Measurement and instrumentation requirements:
   - All services must emit standardized metrics: request_count, request_success, request_latency_ms (histogram), backend_errors, cpu_utilization, gpu_utilization, queue_depth.
   - Metrics must be labeled with service, region, model_version, route.
   - Dashboards: per-service SLO dashboard with burn-rate visualization and 30/90/365-day trend.

## Capacity planning
Objectives: ensure predictable throughput for hosted and dedicated offerings while minimizing cost.

1) Data inputs for planning:
   - Historical traffic by route and region (1/7/30/90 day windows).
   - Per-request consumption (tokens, compute-time, GPU memory).
   - Model performance profiles (throughput per-GPU, batch-scaling curves).
   - Business forecasts (sales commitments, expected customer onboards).

2) Planning process (quarterly + on-demand for launches):
   - Step 1: Gather telemetry and growth forecasts.
   - Step 2: Produce per-service capacity projection (requests per second, GPU-hours) for next 90/180 days.
   - Step 3: Map required capacity to instance types and regions using model performance profiles and autoscaling policies.
   - Step 4: Produce procurement and budgeting request (if reserved instances or Dedicated pools needed).
   - Step 5: Publish capacity plan with clear owners and contingency headroom (default 20% headroom for burst traffic).

3) Autoscaling and throttling rules:
   - Prefer horizontal scaling at frontends and batching layers.
   - Batching policy: maximum batch latency 50 ms for low-latency routes; for high-throughput routes allow configurable batching windows up to 200 ms.
   - Set throttles by route with graceful degradation policies (prioritize high-tier customers; circuit-breaker for uncontrolled tail latencies).

## Reliability initiatives and prioritization
- Quarterly reliability roadmap should be maintained under eng-sre/roadmap. Typical initiatives include: improved KV-cache persistence, prefix caching for common prompts, GPU kernel optimization, automated rollback workflows, and SLO-driven ticketing.
- Prioritization criteria: impact to error budget, user impact severity, operational cost reduction, and deployment risk.
- Small reliability maintenance items (<4 engineer-days) should be scheduled into the next sprint; larger projects into a quarterly reliability track.

## Incident review standards (post-incident process)
1) Triage and timeline:
   - Incident commander opens an incident doc within 1 hour of detection with timeline, scope, and preliminary mitigation.
   - Capture key events (detection, mitigations, communications, root cause hypothesis).

2) Root cause analysis (RCA) requirements:
   - RCAs must include: impact summary, timeline, technical root cause, contributing factors, detection gap, mitigation gap, and three concrete remediation actions with owners and ETA.
   - Severity classification and incident severity must be recorded (SEV1/SEV2/SEV3) with rationale.
   - Use blameless language and focus on system fixes and process improvements.

3) Review cadence and follow-up:
   - Postmortem must be published within 7 calendar days for SEV1/SEV2 and within 14 days for SEV3.
   - A follow-up review is scheduled with stakeholders within 14 days to verify remediation progress.
   - Closed-loop verification: remediation must include a test or metric that will be used to confirm problem resolution.

## Operational tooling and dashboards
Required tools and dashboards (minimum):
- SLO dashboard (per-service) with burn-rate, error-rate, latency distributions.
- On-call runbook index (central runbook listing by service).
- Capacity planning workbook (automated export from metrics + model profiles).
- Incident playbook templates and postmortem template in Confluence.
- Automated alerts: paging for SEV1/SEV2; Slack notifications for lower severities.
- Canary and rollout observability: traffic split metrics, model-variant error deltas, and regression detection.

Suggested integrations:
- Metrics: Prometheus/Thanos (or equivalent) for high-cardinality metrics.
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry with sampled traces for tail-latency analysis.
- Logs: centralized ELK/Cloud logging with retention aligned to compliance policy.
- On-call: PagerDuty (or equivalent) with escalation policies.

## Canonical SRE runbooks (high-level)
Below are canonical runbooks that must be present for each public service. Owners must review monthly and after any major deployment.

Runbook: High error-rate on inference endpoint
1. Detect: Alert triggers when 1-minute error rate > 3x rolling baseline and p95 latency > threshold.
2. Triage: Identify affected routes, model_version, and regions. Check recent deploys and config changes.
3. Mitigate: a) Scale up frontend and batching workers. b) If errors persist, reduce traffic to affected model_version via routing policy (route to fallback model). c) If deployment suspected, roll back last deploy.
4. Restore: Validate success-rate recovery to SLO for 30 minutes before closing.
5. Post-incident: Open RCA and assign remediation actions.

Runbook: Sustained high tail-latency
1. Detect: Alert when p99 latency exceeds SLO and sustained for 5 minutes.
2. Triage: Check GPU utilization, queue depths, batching windows, and kernel errors.
3. Mitigate: Increase batching concurrency or adjust batching window (if safe), add worker capacity, or route traffic to lower-latency model variant.
4. Restore: Monitor p99 to return below threshold for 15 minutes.

Runbook: GPU node offline / hardware failure
1. Detect: Node gone, pods evicted, or high OOM/kube node NotReady alerts.
2. Triage: Identify affected pools and workloads. Check recent node maintenance or provisioning changes.
3. Mitigate: Drain traffic from node, spin up replacement nodes from autoscaler. For Dedicated customers, notify account owner within 15 minutes and provide remediation ETA.
4. Restore: Rebalance KV cache and warm model caches on new nodes.

Runbook: Control-plane degraded (routing/orchestration)
1. Detect: Failure to allocate new inference workers or persistent queue backlog.
2. Triage: Identify errors in control-plane logs, DB connectivity, and message broker.
3. Mitigate: Switch to disaster-mode: fallback to simpler routing (static mapping), reduce non-critical jobs, and notify customers with status page.

## On-call and ownership
- Every service must declare: primary on-call, secondary on-call, owner, and escalation manager.
- On-call responsibilities: respond to pages within the target time (SEV1: 5 minutes, SEV2: 15 minutes), update incident docs, and coordinate mitigations.
- Rota hygiene: handoff notes required for every shift change.

## Templates and artifacts (appendix)
- Incident doc template: Title, severity, timeline, impact, mitigations, follow-ups, owners.
- RCA checklist: data collection, hypothesis validation, contributory factors, remediation plan.
- SLO sign-off template: business owner approval, target, measurement method, and SLAs if applicable.

## Ownership and governance
- eng-sre maintains this document. Service owners must align SLOs with product leads and update SLO definitions annually or on major architectural change.
- Any deviation from the standard error budget policy requires sign-off from SRE manager and Product.

## FAQs
Q: How often are SLOs revisited?
A: At least annually, or after any SEV1 incident that indicates SLO mismatch.

Q: What if a Dedicated customer requires a stricter SLO?
A: Treat as a special-case SLO with a corresponding SLA; document differences and ensure monitoring and compensation are set up.
